## Today

Today's job: predict a county's median household income. We'll fit a line, read its slope in dollars, and check where it misses. You'll use the same tools in [Lab 7](/assignment/07-assignment.html).

We'll use `lm()` for the arithmetic. The harder part is saying what the answer means.

# Start with a prediction {#start-with-a-prediction}

Pick a county. You know the share of adults who have a college degree. Can you make a decent guess about household income?

**Make your guess before you scroll:** Do counties with more college graduates tend to have higher incomes? How closely do you expect the dots to follow that pattern?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Higher college shares generally go with higher incomes. Look at Ingham and Ottawa, though: similar college shares, very different incomes.](07b_files/figure-html/county-income-opening-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='A scatterplot of college attainment and median household income for U.S. counties. The relationship is positive with substantial scatter. Michigan counties are orange, and Ingham and Ottawa are labeled.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Ingham has the larger college share. Ottawa has the higher income. Education helps us predict income across counties, but it can't settle every comparison. Let's fit a line and see how much it helps.

## The data and its units

We'll use the **U.S. Census Bureau's [2020–2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-5year.html)**. The Census Bureau combines five years of survey responses to produce these estimates. All incomes use [2024 inflation-adjusted dollars](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/guidance/comparing-acs-data/2024.html).

Download the prepared file:

- [{{< fa file-arrow-down >}} `county_education_income_2024.csv`](/data/county_education_income_2024.csv)
- [Source tables, variable codes, and preparation notes](/data/county_education_income_2024_source.json)

The file has 3,144 counties and county equivalents in the 50 states and D.C. One county has no usable income estimate. That leaves **3,143 counties** for our examples. All three regressions use these same rows.

| Variable | Meaning | Units |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `CollegePct` | Adults age 25+ with a bachelor's degree or more | Percent, from 0 to 100 |
| `IncomeK` | Median household income | Thousands of 2024 dollars |
| `PovertyPct` | Residents below the poverty threshold, among those for whom poverty status is determined | Percent |
| `MedianAge` | Median age of residents | Years |
| `Population` | Total population estimate | People |
| `CountyFIPS` | County identifier | A five-character code, including leading zeros |

**Each dot represents a whole county.** The median is the income of the middle household when we sort households from lowest to highest income. Households within that county can earn much more or much less.

We give each county the same weight in these regressions. A tiny county gets as much say in the fit as Wayne County.

### Load it


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(GGally)     # Scatterplot matrices
```
:::


If you saved the CSV in your `data` folder, load it like this:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/county_education_income_2024.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    CountyFIPS = col_character(),
    StateFIPS = col_character()
  )
)
```
:::


You can also load the course copy directly:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_raw <- read_csv(
  "https://ec242.netlify.app/data/county_education_income_2024.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    CountyFIPS = col_character(),
    StateFIPS = col_character()
  )
)
```
:::


Keep FIPS codes as text. Otherwise, R can drop a leading `0` from a code. Next, remove rows that lack either variable in our first model:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
counties <- county_raw %>%
  drop_na(CollegePct, IncomeK)

counties %>%
  select(County, State, CollegePct, IncomeK) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  County         State   CollegePct IncomeK
  <chr>          <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Autauga County Alabama      29.1     72.5
2 Baldwin County Alabama      33.7     78.8
3 Barbour County Alabama      10.6     46.0
4 Bibb County    Alabama      11.7     52.5
5 Blount County  Alabama      15.8     64.2
6 Bullock County Alabama       8.12    31.3
```


:::
:::


Here's the code for a simple version of that scatterplot:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(counties, aes(x = CollegePct, y = IncomeK)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "College-educated adults (%)",
       y = "Median household income ($1,000s)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::


::: {.callout-note title="TRY IT: Check the Michigan numbers"}
1. Filter the data to Michigan.
2. Find Ingham and Ottawa. Compare their college shares and incomes.
3. If income always rose with college share, which county would have the higher income? Does it?
:::

# Give the line a job {#give-the-line-a-job}

Start with the lowest-effort guess: give every county the same prediction. Use the **average of the county median incomes**, about $67,976. We'll call this our **baseline**.

Careful with that number. We averaged county medians. We didn't calculate the national median household income.

Now use `CollegePct` to let the prediction change from county to county. Does that beat our one-size-fits-all guess?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Left: one prediction for everyone. Right: the prediction changes with college share. The sloped line makes smaller total squared errors. We'll calculate those errors below.](07b_files/figure-html/county-baseline-versus-line-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two versions of the same county scatterplot. One has a horizontal line at the average county income; the other has an upward-sloping fitted regression line.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Here are the slope and intercept formulas from [Tuesday](/content/Week_07/07a.html#the-regression-line):

$$
\widehat{\beta}_1 = r\frac{s_Y}{s_X},
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y}-\widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}.
$$

The correlation tells us the direction and strength of the linear relationship. Multiplying by $s_Y/s_X$ gives the slope its units: units of `Y` per unit of `X`.

Translate the formulas into R:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
line_by_hand <- counties %>%
  summarize(
    mean_x = mean(CollegePct),
    mean_y = mean(IncomeK),
    sd_x = sd(CollegePct),
    sd_y = sd(IncomeK),
    r = cor(CollegePct, IncomeK)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    slope = r * sd_y / sd_x,
    intercept = mean_y - slope * mean_x
  )

line_by_hand %>% select(r, intercept, slope)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 3
      r intercept slope
  <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>
1 0.720      37.3  1.24
```


:::
:::


The line must pass through $(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})$, the point at the two sample means. Once we have the slope, the intercept formula puts the line through that point.

## Fit the same line with `lm()` {#fit-with-lm}

That was the long route. For everyday use, let `lm()` fit the line:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
education_model <- lm(IncomeK ~ CollegePct, data = counties)
coef(education_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  CollegePct 
      37.27        1.24 
```


:::
:::


Read the formula from left to right:

- `IncomeK` is the **response**, or `Y`: the quantity we want to predict.
- `~` means "modeled as a function of."
- `CollegePct` is the **predictor**, or `X`.
- `data = counties` tells R where to find the columns.

We say that income is **regressed on** education. Keep the order straight. Predicting income from education asks a different question from predicting education from income. Swapping the variables changes the regression line, even though the correlation stays the same.

Save the model as `education_model`. Use `coef()` to pull out its **coefficients**: the intercept and slope.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
b0 <- coef(education_model)[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 <- coef(education_model)[["CollegePct"]]

c(intercept = b0, slope = b1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
intercept     slope 
    37.27      1.24 
```


:::
:::


Same answers as before, with less typing. Our fitted equation is approximately

$$
\widehat{\text{IncomeK}}
= 37.27 + 1.244\times\text{CollegePct}.
$$

The hat means **fitted or predicted**. For a given college share, the line estimates the average county median income. Actual counties can sit above or below that estimate.

# Interpret it in dollars {#interpret-the-slope}

A one-unit increase in `CollegePct` means **one percentage point**: from 30% to 31%, for example. Keep "percentage point" in your explanation. It saves a lot of confusion.

Read the slope like this:

> A one-percentage-point increase in a county's college share corresponds to about **$1,244 more** in predicted median household income.

We're comparing counties here. This slope can't tell us how much one person's income would change if they earned a degree.

## Example 1: A ten-point difference

Going from 30% to 40% is a ten-percentage-point difference. Multiply the slope by ten:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
10 * b1 * 1000
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12436
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Move ten percentage points right. Then move up to the line. That rise is ten times the slope. Both orange dots are predictions; neither represents an actual county.](07b_files/figure-html/county-slope-walk-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='A county scatterplot with a fitted line and an orange right-angle step between predicted incomes at college shares of 30 and 40 percent. The step labels the ten-point education change and its corresponding fitted income change.' width=100%}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note title="TRY IT: Fix this sentence"}
A classmate writes: "Getting a college degree raises household income by $1,244."

Find two problems with that claim. Then rewrite it using what our county model can tell us.
:::

## Example 2: Make a prediction with `predict()`

What income does the line predict at `CollegePct = 30`? Plug in 30:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(b0 + b1 * 30) * 1000
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 74579
```


:::
:::


Use `predict()` to do several values at once. Put the values in a new table. Its predictor column must have **the same name** as the predictor in the model:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
new_counties <- tibble(CollegePct = c(30, 40))

new_counties %>%
  mutate(predicted_income_dollars =
           1000 * predict(education_model, newdata = new_counties))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  CollegePct predicted_income_dollars
       <dbl>                    <dbl>
1         30                   74579.
2         40                   87015.
```


:::
:::


We fit the model with `IncomeK`, so `predict()` returns thousands of dollars. Multiply by 1,000 to get dollars. R won't do that conversion for you.

### What about the intercept?

The intercept gives the prediction at `CollegePct = 0`: about $37,271. Before we build a story around it, check the data. The college shares range from about 0% to 80.5%.

Exactly one county has a zero in this file: Loving County, Texas. Its estimated population is 33. That's a thin basis for a grand theory about places with no college graduates.

Here, the intercept mainly sets the line's position. In other datasets, zero may fall outside the data entirely.

## Example 3: Change the units, keep the relationship

Now fit the same model with income in dollars instead of thousands of dollars:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dollar_model <- lm(MedianIncome ~ CollegePct, data = counties)

coef(education_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  CollegePct 
      37.27        1.24 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
coef(dollar_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  CollegePct 
      37271        1244 
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Same dots, same line, different labels. Measuring income in dollars makes both coefficients 1,000 times larger. The correlation and R-squared stay the same.](07b_files/figure-html/county-units-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='The same fitted county relationship shown with income measured in thousands of dollars and in dollars. The lines have the same visual shape, while the reported slopes differ by a factor of one thousand.' width=100%}
:::
:::


A bigger coefficient doesn't earn bragging rights. A slope of 1.244 and a slope of 1,243.6 describe the same relationship here. **Report the units with the number.**

# Look at the mistakes {#residuals}

How far did the prediction miss? Subtract the fitted income from the observed income. For county $i$, that difference is the **residual**:

$$
e_i = Y_i-\widehat{Y}_i.
$$

- A positive residual means observed income is above the line: we **underpredicted**.
- A negative residual means observed income is below the line: we **overpredicted**.

Use `fitted()` for the predictions and `resid()` for the residuals:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_results <- counties %>%
  mutate(
    fitted_income = fitted(education_model),
    residual = resid(education_model)
  )

county_results %>%
  filter(State == "Michigan",
         County %in% c("Ingham County", "Ottawa County", "Washtenaw County")) %>%
  select(County, IncomeK, fitted_income, residual)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  County           IncomeK fitted_income residual
  <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Ingham County       65.5          88.5   -23.0 
2 Ottawa County       90.5          85.7     4.84
3 Washtenaw County    89.2         110.    -21.1 
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Read each orange gap vertically: observed income minus fitted income. A gap tells us how far the model missed. It can't tell us why.](07b_files/figure-html/county-residual-segments-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='The education-income scatterplot with vertical orange segments between the fitted line and the observed values for Ingham, Ottawa, and Washtenaw counties. Labels show signed residuals.' width=100%}
:::
:::


The model guesses too high for Ingham and too low for Ottawa. What did it miss? Maybe household composition matters. Maybe industries, housing costs, or age matter.

Those are leads to investigate. We can't pick the winning explanation from a residual alone.

::: {.callout-note title="TRY IT: Find a county the line misses"}
1. Use `county_results` to find the largest **positive** residual in Michigan.
2. Find the most negative residual.
3. For each, report the observed value, fitted value, and residual in dollars.
4. Explain which county the model underpredicts and which it overpredicts.
:::

## Why this line? Squared errors {#squared-errors}

Add up the raw residuals and positive misses can cancel negative ones. Square them first. Now every nonzero miss adds to the total, and big misses count much more than small ones.

**Ordinary least squares (OLS)** chooses the intercept and slope with the smallest **sum of squared errors**, or SSE:

$$
\text{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\widehat{Y}_i)^2.
$$

Try three slopes. For each one, put the line through the two sample means. That gives each slope its best possible intercept.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![OLS wins this comparison: it has the smallest squared-error total. The labels report RMSE, which puts the errors back in income units and ranks these lines in the same order.](07b_files/figure-html/county-squared-loss-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three county scatterplots with a line that is too flat, the OLS line, and a line that is too steep. Each panel reports its root mean squared error, with the smallest value for OLS.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Squared dollars are awkward to read. **Root mean squared error (RMSE)** puts the error measure back in the units of income. Average the squared residuals, then take the square root:

$$
\text{RMSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2}.
$$

Our one-size-fits-all baseline has an RMSE of about **$17,772**. Adding education brings that down to about **$12,338**.

That's an improvement on the data we used to fit the line. To check predictions for new counties, we'd need to test the model on data we held out.

## Did we beat the baseline? {#r-squared}

$R^2$ reports the share of the baseline's squared error that our line removes:

$$
R^2
=1-\frac{\sum_i(Y_i-\widehat{Y}_i)^2}
          {\sum_i(Y_i-\bar{Y})^2}.
$$


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sse_model <- sum(resid(education_model)^2)
sse_baseline <- sum((counties$IncomeK - mean(counties$IncomeK))^2)

1 - sse_model / sse_baseline
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.518
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(education_model)$r.squared
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.518
```


:::
:::


Here, $R^2$ is about **51.8%**. Compared with our baseline, the line cuts total squared error by that share.

Don't read that as "education causes 52% of income" or "we got 52% of counties exactly right." $R^2$ measures a reduction in squared error.

For a simple OLS regression with an intercept, $R^2$ also equals the sample correlation squared. Conveniently, the name checks out.

## Check where the line misses


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Left: check how the residuals change as fitted income rises. Right: check the size and spread of the misses. Several counties earn much more than the line predicts.](07b_files/figure-html/county-residual-diagnostics-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='A residual-versus-fitted scatterplot and a histogram of residuals for the county education model, both with zero reference lines.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Look at the long positive tail. Our model makes some very large underpredictions. A decent $R^2$ leaves plenty of room for those.

# Two more worked examples {#more-examples}

Keep income as the response. Keep the same counties. Try a different predictor.

## Example 4: A negative slope

What do you expect if we regress median household income on the poverty rate?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
poverty_model <- lm(IncomeK ~ PovertyPct, data = counties)
coef(poverty_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  PovertyPct 
      98.80       -2.17 
```


:::
:::


A one-percentage-point higher poverty rate is associated with about **$2,167 lower** fitted median household income.

There's a reason this relationship is strong: both variables describe the county's incomes. The poverty rate already tells us something about who has low income. We're describing the same period here, so don't treat this as a forecast of future income.

## Example 5: Age doesn't get us very far

Could median age help? Older residents may earn more after years in the workforce. Retired households may earn less. The stories point in different directions. Let's check the data:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
age_model <- lm(IncomeK ~ MedianAge, data = counties)
coef(age_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)   MedianAge 
     82.383      -0.344 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(age_model)$r.squared
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.011
```


:::
:::


Median age barely improves on the baseline. R still returns a slope, of course. Ask for a line and you'll get a line. You have to decide whether it helps.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Education slopes up. Poverty slopes down. Both beat the age model by a lot. Each panel shows a separate regression with one predictor.](07b_files/figure-html/county-three-predictors-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three county scatterplots: income rises with college attainment, falls with poverty, and has a weak relationship with median age. Each panel gives its own slope and R-squared.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Check the far-right end of the poverty plot. The line predicts negative income. All the observed incomes are positive. Ope. The model misses that part of the pattern badly, despite its respectable $R^2$.

::: {.callout-note title="TRY IT: Compare the models"}
1. Which model has the larger $R^2$: education or poverty?
2. Does a negative slope mean a model is bad?
3. Would comparing the absolute slopes of the age and education models tell us which is more useful? Check their units before answering.
:::

# Explore several relationships {#scatterplot-matrices}

Four variables give us six pairs to inspect. A **scatterplot matrix** puts them in one figure:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_numeric <- counties %>%
  select(CollegePct, IncomeK, PovertyPct, MedianAge)

ggpairs(
  county_numeric,
  columnLabels = c("College (%)", "Income ($1,000s)", "Poverty (%)", "Median age"),
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.12, size = 0.4)),
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", stars = FALSE, size = 4))
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Scan one pair at a time. The diagonal shows distributions, the lower panels show scatterplots, and the upper panels report correlations. Open a full-size scatterplot when a pair catches your eye.](07b_files/figure-html/county-pairs-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='A four-by-four scatterplot matrix for college attainment, income, poverty, and median age, with distributions on the diagonal and correlations in the upper triangle.' width=100%}
:::
:::


**Don't feed an ID code into `cor()` just because R stored it as a number.** FIPS codes identify places. They are not measurements of how much "county" a place has.

## A compact correlation picture


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_cor <- cor(county_numeric)
round(county_cor, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           CollegePct IncomeK PovertyPct MedianAge
CollegePct       1.00    0.72      -0.46     -0.10
IncomeK          0.72    1.00      -0.73     -0.10
PovertyPct      -0.46   -0.73       1.00     -0.17
MedianAge       -0.10   -0.10      -0.17      1.00
```


:::
:::


Turn those numbers into a heatmap and you have a **correlogram**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![We only need one triangle: swapping X and Y gives the same correlation. The diagonal would be all ones. Income's correlations with education and poverty are about equally strong, with opposite signs.](07b_files/figure-html/county-correlogram-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='A triangular correlation heatmap for college attainment, income, poverty, and median age, with numeric correlations printed in each tile.' width=100%}
:::
:::


<details class="collapsible-bg">
<summary><strong>Show me how to build the heatmap with ggplot</strong></summary>

First, turn the matrix into a long table with one row per pair. `as.table()` keeps the row and column labels. `as.data.frame()` puts them into columns.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(county_cor)) %>%
  rename(variable_x = Var1, variable_y = Var2, correlation = Freq) %>%
  filter(as.integer(variable_x) < as.integer(variable_y))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(variable_x, variable_y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#D9A27F", mid = "white", high = "#8DB4A3",
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::


The `filter()` step keeps one triangle and drops the diagonal. Keep the numbers visible. Color helps us scan; the labels tell us what we're looking at.

</details>

# Four ways to fool yourself {#check-the-line}

Before you trust a line, check the scatterplot, unusual points, prediction range, and sample. Here's how each can trip us up.

## 1. A curve can hide from correlation


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![These dots are simulated. The U-shape is easy to see, but its correlation is near zero. One straight line can't follow the drop and the rise.](07b_files/figure-html/regression-curved-patterns-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Simulated positive, negative, and U-shaped relationships. Orange straight-line fits follow the first two patterns but miss the curve, whose correlation is near zero.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Correlation measures a **linear** relationship. A small correlation can send you right past a strong curve. Plot the dots before you declare "nothing going on here."

::: {.callout-note title="TRY IT: Predict before calculating"}
Start at the left edge of the U. Move toward zero. What happens to Y? Now move from zero to the right edge. What changes? Explain why one slope can't describe both parts well.
:::

## 2. Some points pull the line harder


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![These examples are simulated. Left: a large residual near the mean of X barely changes the slope. Right: a point far out on X pulls the slope sharply. Check unusual points before deciding what to do with them.](07b_files/figure-html/regression-influence-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two simulated datasets compare a high-residual point near the center of X with a high-residual point far outside the other X values. Original and refitted lines show a much larger slope change in the second case.' width=100%}
:::
:::


A **large residual** means the line missed that observation by a lot. An **influential point** changes the fitted line by a lot when we include it. The pictures show why those can differ.

Inspect an unusual point. Check its units and source. Find out what it represents. "It ruined my beautiful regression" is not a data-cleaning rule.

Check who the prediction is for, too. We fit this model to counties. Using it as a salary calculator for one graduate would change the question completely.

## 4. Change the sample, change the slope

Remember sampling variation from last week? It applies to slopes, too. Choose a different set of counties and you'll usually get a different line.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Each orange line uses a separate sample of 50 counties, drawn without replacement. Green uses the full file. This exercise shows what changes when we select different counties. The ACS survey margins of error are a separate source of uncertainty.](07b_files/figure-html/county-sampling-variation-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Eight orange regression lines estimated from separate samples of fifty counties, overlaid on the county scatterplot. A thicker green line shows the fit using the full county file.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Try a sample of 50:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(15)

small_sample <- counties %>% slice_sample(n = 50)
small_model <- lm(IncomeK ~ CollegePct, data = small_sample)

coef(small_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  CollegePct 
      31.75        1.52 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
coef(education_model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)  CollegePct 
      37.27        1.24 
```


:::
:::


Compare the two sets of coefficients. The small-sample slope won't exactly match the full-file slope. We'll put numbers on that uncertainty in a later lesson.
